Notes on the March relay outage

These are my working notes from the week after the outage, written for the
people who were not on the call. They are long because the short version has
already gone round and left most of the interesting questions unanswered.

What customers saw

For a little over two hours on Saturday morning, deliveries to a small group
of tenants arrived late or not at all. Nothing was lost in the end, because
the outbox kept every event and the relay caught up once it was healthy, but
several customers build billing workflows on top of these events and a late
event is, for them, the same as a wrong one. Two of them noticed before we
did. That alone is worth a section of its own further down.

How it started

The trigger was ordinary. A customer endpoint began answering slowly, then
stopped answering. The relay is designed for this and has been for years. It
retries with increasing delays, and after enough failures it parks the event
where an operator can look at it. What changed this time is that the endpoint
belonged to a tenant who had recently been moved to a much higher sending
limit, and nobody had revisited the retry settings for a tenant of that size.

With the old limit, a dead endpoint produced a trickle of retries. With the
new one it produced a flood. Each retry held a worker for the full timeout,
the worker pool is shared between tenants, and within a few minutes every
worker was waiting on the same unreachable host. Healthy tenants queued up
behind it. From the outside the whole relay looked slow, although only one
destination in several thousand was actually broken.

Why the alarms stayed quiet

We alert on the rate of failed deliveries and on the age of the oldest event
in the outbox. Neither moved quickly enough. Failures were not being recorded
as failures, because a request that is still waiting has not failed yet. The
outbox age did climb, but the threshold had been raised a few months earlier
after a noisy week, and it now sat well above anything a customer would
tolerate. Both decisions were reasonable when they were made. Together they
left a gap wide enough for two hours to pass through.

The first page came from a person, not a monitor. A support engineer saw the
second customer message, recognised the pattern from the first, and woke the
person on call. I would like to say that our tooling would have caught it a
few minutes later. I do not believe that it would have.

What we did on the day

The person on call found the saturated pool within ten minutes, which is a
credit to the dashboards, and then spent most of an hour trying the wrong
remedy. Restarting the relay cleared the workers, and for a short while
everything looked healthy. Then the outbox replayed, the same events were
picked up again, and the pool filled exactly as before. This happened three
times. Each restart also reset the retry counters, so the events that should
have been parked after a handful of attempts were instead given a fresh start
every time.

The fix that worked was manual and unglamorous. We paused sending for the one
tenant, let the pool drain, and watched the backlog for everyone else clear
in about twenty minutes. The affected tenant was told directly, their
endpoint came back that afternoon, and we released their events in batches.

What I think we should change

First, workers should not be shared without limit. A single tenant should
never be able to occupy more than a fixed share of the pool, whatever their
sending limit says. This is the change that would have turned the outage into
a slow afternoon for one customer and nothing at all for the rest.

Second, the retry counter has to survive a restart. It lives in memory today
because that was simple, and because a restart used to be rare. It is no
longer rare, and an operator reaching for a restart during an incident should
not be quietly undoing the one protection that was working.

Third, a raised sending limit should come with a review of everything that
scales with it. We have a checklist for lowering limits and none for raising
them, which says something about where we expected trouble to come from.

Fourth, and this is the one I feel most strongly about, we should alert on
what customers experience rather than on what the relay reports about itself.
The age of the oldest undelivered event for each tenant is a number a
customer would recognise. The rate of failed deliveries is not, and on the
day it told us everything was fine.

What I am less sure about

There is an argument that the timeout itself is too generous, and that a
shorter one would have freed workers quickly enough to avoid the pile up. I
am not convinced. Several large customers have endpoints that are slow in
perfectly healthy ways, and a shorter timeout would trade one rare outage for
a steady stream of small ones. I would rather isolate tenants from each other
and leave the timeout alone, but I hold that view loosely and would like to
see the numbers before we decide.

There is also the question of whether the person on call should have paused
the tenant sooner. With hindsight, obviously. At the time, pausing a paying
customer felt like a larger step than restarting a service, and nothing in
our runbook said otherwise. If we want people to take the smaller, safer
action under pressure, the runbook has to say plainly that it is allowed.

Thanks to everyone who gave up their Saturday, and in particular to the
support engineer who connected two messages that the rest of us had treated
as unrelated.
